quiz.title: Matrices Exercise 3.2 Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on the operations from Exercise 3.2 — addition, scalar multiplication, matrix products, order of a product and simple matrix equations. Choose an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: NCERT Class 12 Maths, Matrices Exercise 3.2 (operations on matrices)

questions.explanation: Add matrices entry by entry: 1+2=3, 2+0=2, 3+1=4, 4+5=9, giving [[3, 2], [4, 9]].
Scalar multiplication multiplies every entry by 3: 3, -6, 0 and 12.

questions.q: If A has order 2 x 3 and B has order 3 x 4, what is the order of the product AB?
questions.explanation: AB is defined because the columns of A (3) equal the rows of B (3). The product keeps the outer dimensions: 2 x 4.

questions.q: For two matrices A and B where both AB and BA are defined and square, which statement is true in general?
options: AB is always equal to BA
AB and BA are never defined together
AB always equals the zero matrix
questions.explanation: Matrix multiplication is not commutative. Even when both products exist and have the same order, AB and BA are usually different.
A 1 x 2 matrix times a 2 x 1 matrix gives a 1 x 1 result: 1(3) + 2(4) = 3 + 8 = 11.

questions.q: If 2X = [[4, 6], [8, 2]], what is the matrix X?
questions.explanation: Divide every entry by 2 (multiply by the scalar 1/2): X = [[2, 3], [4, 1]].

questions.q: If I is the 2 x 2 identity matrix and B is any 2 x 2 matrix, what is IB?
questions.explanation: The identity matrix leaves any matrix unchanged under multiplication, so IB = B (and BI = B as well).

faq.q: When can two matrices be added in Exercise 3.2?
faq.a: Only matrices of the same order can be added. You add corresponding entries, so a 2 x 3 matrix can be added to another 2 x 3 matrix but not to a 3 x 2 one.

faq.q: When is the product AB defined, and what is its order?
faq.a: AB is defined only when the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B. If A is m x n and B is n x p, then AB has order m x p.

faq.q: Why is AB usually not equal to BA?
faq.a: Matrix multiplication is not commutative. Swapping the order changes which rows meet which columns, so AB and BA generally differ — and sometimes only one of them is even defined.

faq.q: How do I solve a matrix equation like 2X = A?
faq.a: Treat the scalar like a number: multiply both sides by 1/2, which means dividing every entry of A by 2. For equations such as A + X = B, subtract A entry by entry to get X = B - A.
